newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul says U.S. man held in N.Korea was missionary.
newsitem.headline: Seoul says U.S. man held in N.Korea was missionary.

text.p: South Korea said on Monday a U.S. citizen held in North Korea on spy charges was a China-based missionary, and it denied allegations he was working for Seoul.
A foreign ministry spokesman said he believed Evan Carl Hunzike was engaged in missionary work in an area of northeast China bordering North Korea.
"My understanding is that he was in China as a missionary," the spokesman said by telephone. He said Hunzike had South Korean ancestry on his mother's side.

Pyongyang said on Sunday Hunzike was arrested on August 24 after crossing the Amnok river, called the Yalu in Chinese, from China and had been charged with spying for the South. The charges carry a possible death penalty.
The foreign ministry spokesman denied Hunzike was a South Korean agent. "We absolutely deny the allegation," he said.
South Korea's Yonhap news agency said Hunzike was in his mid-20s. His father was American.
Deputy U.S. State Department spokesman Glyn Davies, speaking to reporters in Gaza, said: "We deny categorically he is in any way connected with the U.S. government."
The espionage allegations add new fuel to a feud between North and South Korea over the deaths of 22 of 26 North Koreans who landed by submarine in the South last month.

Pyongyang has threatened "merciless retaliation" for the deaths, vowing "blood should be paid for blood", and has demanded Seoul return the vessel along with the survivors and bodies of the dead crew.
South Korean President Kim Young-sam, backed by opposition leaders, on Monday demanded Pyongyang immediately stop threatening reprisals.
A presidential spokesman said that at a crisis meeting, Kim and the opposition politicians "warned North Korea that any provocations would receive stern punishment".
"They also agreed to strengthen police and military forces to better cope with the North's aggressiveness."

Seoul has already stepped up security at airports, ports and diplomatic missions, assigned more bodyguards to key public figures and tightened vigilance on five west coast islands seen as most vulnerable to a northern attack.
Pyongyang on Monday again accused Seoul of provoking conflict on the tense Korean peninsula, where a fragile ceasefire has kept the peace since the 1950-53 Korean War.

"Their frantic arms buildup, confrontation and adventurous war gambles against the North may lead to a war provocation against the North any time in league with outsiders," the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.

"The Kim Young-sam bellicose group must act with discretion, clearly mindful that if they dare unleash a war against the North, like a puppy knowing no fear of the tiger, they will be annihilated," KCNA quoted a commentary in the Rodong Sinmun newspaper as saying.
Yonhap said Pyongyang had asked Washington in mid-September to confirm the identity of the alleged spy.
Washington has asked the Swedish charge d'affaires in Pyongyang, which represents U.S. interests in North Korea, to help gather information on the espionage charges.

"The charge of the Swedish embassy in Pyongyang is making enquiries on behalf of the United States on the status of this individual," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters in Buffalo, New York.
Analysts view the spy charges as part of efforts by Pyongyang to divert attention from the submarine incident by creating a new crisis.
